name: David Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior buyer at Allbrook Motor Factors. We supply brake pads, filters, batteries and the like to about 400 independent garages. I'm in at seven, and the first hour is on the phone with the manufacturers' reps, because I like to hear a voice before I place an order. Then I go through the stock sheets with the warehouse manager Terry, and I walk the shelves. Afternoons are for the garages that ring me directly, because they know I'll tell them the truth about lead times.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I like is that it's concrete. A bad decision turns up as a pallet of the wrong wipers sitting in the corner. What wears me out is the endless new systems head office buys and then abandons. My wife Gail works part-time at a dental surgery, and she says I come home and complain about a screen I've been staring at all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. I call this one "AI Plateau". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to them. At work I'd say show me a price it gets that I can't. Down the pub I'd say it's another bubble, like the ones before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it changes nothing for me, which is what I want. I've got about five years and I'd like them quiet. Trouble is that things are not quiet for other reasons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. Same phone calls, same shelves, same reps. I'd put away what I can each month and check my pension forecast again, because I'm not sure the company is as steady as it was. I'd probably retire at 63 if nothing odd happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, to be straight. Not about the machines. About the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said uneasy but not about AI. What's on your mind at Allbrook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Allbrook's competition is an online parts platform that undercuts us on the common lines. Our garages are loyal, but loyalty has limits when the other lot is 8 per cent cheaper. If they lose the margin war, my pension pot will be fine, but my job won't be so safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI saves a bit of time, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was proven and my boss told me to, I'd try it for a week. But I'd not rush. I've watched a so-called smart ordering system we bought in 2016 order 600 litres of screenwash in July. It took us a year to sell it. Machines don't know the weather the way Terry does.

say: I'd say **good luck to them**, and ask to see a price it gets that I can't.
Down the pub I'd call it another **bubble**.
think: Privately it changes nothing for me, which is what I want, with **five years** to go.
Allbrook's real threat is the **online platform**, not AI.
do: Carry on with the same **phone calls** and shelf walks.
Save what I can monthly and recheck my **pension forecast**, retiring at 63 if nothing odd happens.
feel: **Uneasy**, not about machines but about the firm.
S0.quote: I've watched a so-called smart ordering system we bought in 2016 order 600 litres of screenwash in July.
fieldNote: The **unease** is about Allbrook's margins, a pressure he already carries.
Distrust of systems comes from one specific failure he can name.
Short, dry answers; opens up on concrete stories.

steps.text: Keep the same phone calls and shelf walks with Terry
Save extra each month and recheck the pension forecast

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. I call this one "Steady Disruption". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it will be mixed. At work I'd say let's see it working on one product line before we rely on it. To friends I'd say people exaggerate, but I can see the writing on the wall for jobs that are all screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the reordering is the bit most at risk. That's what I do, in the end: look at sales, look at stock, order. If the software does that, what are they paying me for? Maybe the supplier talk, but a rep would rather speak to a person who can say yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do the work, but I'd watch what happens to the junior buyers. If they start cutting, I'd put my name down for an early exit deal at 61. I'd also tidy our finances, cancel the second car, and think about downsizing the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's a creeping thing. I'm not a worrier, but it's there when I wake at four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your daily jobs could software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, test it on tyres and wipers first, then batteries. If it works, it works, and I'd not stand in the way. But I'd want somebody to be accountable when it orders wrongly, and it wouldn't be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If head office asked you to sign off a software-run reorder system, what would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two lads in my team, Sunil and Jake, are in their twenties and quick with software. They'd probably be fine, or at least they'd be ahead of me. I'd be the one at 58 asked to explain why we still need a buyer who prefers the phone.

say: I'd say **test it** on one product line before relying on it.
To friends I'd say the writing's on the wall for jobs that are **all screens**.
think: Privately reordering is what I do, so it's the part most **at risk**.
At 58 I'd be the buyer asked why we still need someone who likes the **phone**.
do: Keep my head down and watch what happens to the **junior buyers**.
Put my name down for an **early exit** deal at 61, and cancel the second car.
feel: **Anxious**, a creeping feeling that wakes me at four in the morning.
S1.quote: I'd be the one at 58 asked to explain why we still need a buyer who prefers the phone.
fieldNote: Reordering is his core task, so his **anxiety** is realistic.
He is not a worrier by nature, which gives the four a.m. waking weight.
His plan is an early exit, not a fight.

steps.text: Put my name down for an early exit deal at 61
Cancel the second car and trim household spending
Ask Allbrook to test software on tyres and wipers first

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. I call this one "AGI by 2028". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready, and don't pretend. At work I'd say we'll ride it out together. Down the pub I'd say the people in charge need to get a grip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my job's gone. All of buying is thinking work, which is exactly what this thing does. I'm not young enough to learn something new and not old enough to stop, which is the worst age. Three years to retirement would feel like a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the pension adviser first week. Then I'd talk to Allbrook about an early exit at 60, and be ready to take a lower payout. We'd stop the holidays, cut the car, and think about selling the family house, which is too big now that Marek and Anna have gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd have it on my mind all the time, even though we've got savings. It's not the money, it's what I'd do with myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd do with the money side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gail. She'd be steady, because she's calmer than me, and she's got her job. We'd sit at the kitchen table, work out what we have, and what the minimum is. Then I'd ring Marek and Anna and tell them straight, so they don't hear it from someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who'd you want to talk to first, and what would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know who to blame. Not the machine, not the firms, because they'd do the same in their shoes. I'd just say it's the market, and the market doesn't care. It's still a poor way to treat a man who's given thirty years.

say: I'd say **nobody's ready**, so let's not pretend.
Down the pub I'd say the people in charge need to **get a grip**.
think: Privately I think my job's **gone**: all of buying is thinking work.
I'm too old to learn something new and too young to **stop**.
do: See the **pension adviser** in week one, then ask Allbrook for an early exit at 60.
Stop holidays, cut the car and think about selling the **family house**.
feel: **Alarmed**: savings help, but I'd fear what I'd do with myself.
S2.quote: I'm not young enough to learn something new and not old enough to stop, which is the worst age.
fieldNote: The **alarm** is about identity and years, as money is secure.
He is unwilling to assign blame; calls it "the market".
Practical steps come fast: adviser, exit deal, house.

steps.text: Book the pension adviser in the first week
Ask Allbrook for an early exit at 60
Stop holidays and sell the car
Sell the family house and move somewhere smaller

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. I call this one "AGI by 2031". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, but less rotten than two years. At work I'd say let's prepare. Down the pub I'd say it's late to be asking questions now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it lets me get out before it bites. I'd be 63, and I could leave on my pension without a fight. The ones I'd worry for are Sunil and Jake, who'd be mid-career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to 62 or 63, and not a day more. I'd save more, pay off the last bit of the mortgage and put the money towards a smaller place. I'd show Sunil everything I know about the garages, because it's the one thing the firm would lose with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but it's more like waiting for a delayed train. I can plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What shifts for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a crisis. Five is a countdown. I can handle a countdown. I'd know what I'm doing with each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the garages you supply?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'll go the way of the corner shop. Big garages with software will survive, small ones will be squeezed. I'd feel bad about the old boys who've bought from me for thirty years, but I can't save them.

say: I'd say it's too fast but **less rotten** than two years.
Down the pub I'd say it's late to be asking the questions.
think: Privately it lets me **get out** before it bites, on my pension at 63.
I'd worry about Sunil and Jake, who'd be **mid-career**.
do: Work to **62 or 63** and no later.
Pay off the last of the mortgage and **hand Sunil** everything I know about the garages.
feel: **Anxious**, but like waiting for a delayed train, and I can plan around it.
S3.quote: Two years is a crisis. Five is a countdown. I can handle a countdown.
fieldNote: Five years turns panic into a **countdown**, but he still expects the job to go.
Mood stays at alarmed because the job disappears before his pension is fully safe.
Mentoring Sunil is a duty, not a hope.

steps.text: Pay off the last of the mortgage
Teach Sunil what I know about the garages
Look at a smaller place near Anna

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. I call this one "AGI by 2036". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time and people should use it. At work I'd say keep going. Down the pub I'd say wake me in nine years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'll be done before it matters. I'd say most of it is for my children. Marek is an electrician, so he's probably safe a good while. Anna does accounts, and that's thinking work, so I do worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 63 and then stop. In the meantime I'd keep saving, and I'd buy a small rental flat with the lump sum, which would give us a bit of income. I'd also help Anna look at ways to do something that's harder to automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, at most. It's a worry about the next generation, and that's part of being a dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be retired well before 2036. Does the ten-year picture touch you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to Anna, think about being the person people trust, not the person who adds up columns. And to Marek, stay in a trade. Hands are going to be the last thing replaced, I'd guess, though nobody knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68 and, I hope, on a boat on the canal with Gail, which she's been after me about. I'd read the paper and moan about the news. And I'd probably still ring Terry every Friday to hear what's happening.

say: I'd say there's time, and people should **use it**.
Down the pub I'd say wake me in nine years.
think: Privately I'll be **done** before it matters, so it's for my children.
Marek's trade seems safe, but Anna's accounts work is **thinking work**.
do: Work until **63**, then buy a small rental flat with the lump sum.
Help Anna look for something **harder to automate**.
feel: **Uneasy** at most, a father's worry for the next generation.
S4.quote: I'd say to Anna, think about being the person people trust, not the person who adds up columns.
fieldNote: Distance **softens** him: the worry becomes fatherly.
Small property investment gives income without risk.
His quote shows a dry, practical advice style, aimed at his daughter's accounts career and her future.

steps.text: Buy a small rental flat with the lump sum
Help Anna find a role built on trust

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because it leaves me three years from the finish line with no job. What would help is a decent early-retirement deal, a pension nobody can touch, and a bit of notice. I don't ask for much. I'd like to leave on my own terms, and with my name still meaning something.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not against the new stuff. I'm slow to trust it. I'd like someone to explain a system to me before it takes my desk, and to say what it's meant to do.

headlineQuote: I'd like to leave on my own terms, and with my name still meaning something.
portrait: David is a **58-year-old** senior buyer of car parts at a distributor serving 400 independent garages, and he never uses AI tools.
He is a dry, pragmatic centrist who trusts phone calls and shelf walks, and distrusts systems after a screenwash disaster.
His job is mostly reordering, so he moves from uneasy to **alarmed** as the timeline shortens, even with savings.
He blames the market rather than any person, and plans a quiet early exit.
His wife Gail's steady job and their savings let him choose an **early exit**, a smaller home and a rental flat.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most, leaving him three years from the finish line with no job.
whatWouldHelp: A decent **early-retirement deal**, a protected pension and some notice, so he can leave on his own terms.
